paras: The Liberty County race riot was a wave of attacks on Black residents near Liberty City, Georgia, in August 1900, in which a posse killed a Black man, Charles Small, and white men whipped the occupants of many Black homes after a white man, Robert C. Curtis, was shot dead on August 15. Reports of the Black dead ranged from one to five, and the governor called out militia before the sheriff reported order restored on August 18; wire services called it a "race war."

According to the Savannah Morning News, J. T. Gill held a warrant against Turner Johnson, alias Dotson, for using obscene language before a woman of merchant C. J. McDonald's family. As Gill and Curtis, a clerk from Raleigh, North Carolina, brought Johnson in, Johnson drew a pistol and men hidden in the bushes opened fire, killing Curtis and wounding Gill. It named Johnson, Frank Hines, Ed Shuman, Henry Harris and William Burney as the gunmen and called the shooting a plan "concocted" in advance.

Hines and Allen Cooley were jailed at Hinesville, while the correspondent warned that Sheriff Brewer might not be able to protect prisoners and predicted "bloodshed" if the searching party caught the accused.

On August 16 a posse led by County Bailiff Farmer went to arrest Small, who was accused of breaking the arm of O. W. Tally at Aimar's mill, and shot him to death. In the posse's account, Small swung a club at Farmer; the Savannah paper declared his fate "deserved."

That night white men took Black residents from their homes and whipped them, according to the Savannah correspondent "for incendiary speeches." Other dispatches said many or "a score" of homes were visited and the occupants tied up and beaten, some seriously. The same night a Black man's shoe shop at Liberty City and Gill's store at Walthourville burned, and a rail switch at Aimar's mill was tampered with. White papers blamed Black residents for the fires and an attempted train wreck, though the Savannah correspondent doubted the track had been obstructed.

On August 17 Governor Candler ordered out the Liberty Guards after Deputy Sheriff G. N. Hendry telegraphed "Can't control mob at all" and reported one man taken from the guard and one killed resisting arrest. The wire story said the man taken from the guard "is supposed to have been murdered," which no later report confirmed. Armed citizens and cavalry patrolled Liberty City as women and children left, and Col. James Thomas of a Wayne County posse was accidentally shot. On August 18 Brewer told the governor the Black residents "had dispersed" and troops were no longer needed.

Cooley (spelled Colley) was released on August 19 for lack of evidence, and in September the governor offered a reward for Turner Johnson, Henry Harris and Bill Veney. No report of an inquest into Small's death or of arrests for the whippings was found.

The Savannah Morning News correspondent supplied the fullest reports, printed the posse's version of Small's death, and wrote that other papers' reports were "denounced as unfair and unjust." An Atlanta wire, printed from Kansas to New Mexico, cast the episode as a "Negro Uprising" where "the blacks outnumber the whites three to one." Headlines elsewhere read "Negroes Resist Arrest for Murder and Set Fire to Two Towns," and the Wheeling Register blamed "irresponsible negroes."

A few papers differed: the Sumter Watchman and Southron ran the deputy's telegram under "Negroes Hunted Like Beasts," and the Worcester Spy headed its dispatch "No Negro Rising." Unnamed tolls traveled widely, from five Black dead in the New-York Tribune to "two whites and three negroes" in a Nebraska weekly.
The only Black-press item found, in the Richmond Planet on August 25, reprinted the Atlanta wire without comment.

The Savannah paper named only Small among the Black dead, Hendry's telegram reported one killed and one taken from the guard, the Atlanta wire said two, the Brunswick correspondent three, and the Tribune five. Two dispatches counted two white men killed; only Curtis was named. The Savannah correspondent said Small's death was unconnected with the Curtis killing, while a Liberty City wire called him one of those said to have taken part.

reader.title: Liberty County race riot (1900)
bases: After the shooting of a white man, posses and armed whites killed at least one Black man (Small) and visited and whipped the occupants of many Black homes across the area while patrolling against a feared 'uprising' (A3, A6, A11, A20).

Separate local and special dispatches agree that a posse killed Charles Small and that whites whipped Black residents in their homes on the night of Aug. 16-17 (A3, A6, A11, A20), though the number of Black dead is disputed (A4, A10, A11).

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News correspondent at Liberty City
accounts.gist: Curtis was ambushed by Johnson's friends in a planned attack; Small was a 'dangerous character' killed while resisting a posse, unconnected with Curtis; whippings were for 'incendiary speeches'; the correspondent doubted the train obstructions were real.

accounts.label: Deputy Sheriff Hendry's telegram and the Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: Accused men were joined in the woods by others; towns were fired and the railroad torn up; one man was taken from the guard and one killed resisting arrest; 'Can't control mob at all.'

accounts.label: Liberty City and Washington Times specials
accounts.gist: Five Black men had been killed; whites 'seeking revenge' visited huts and whipped the occupants after fires attributed to Black residents.

accounts.label: Brunswick/Jesup correspondent
accounts.gist: Two whites and three blacks killed since Wednesday; Black residents organizing in the swamps; posses and rifles sent in.

accounts.label: Richmond Planet column
accounts.gist: Reprinted the Atlanta wire: one white man killed, two Black men reported killed for resisting arrest, a 'race war' under way.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News printed the posse's account and said of Small 'His fate was deserved,' and described the Curtis killing as 'a deliberate plan.'
The Atlanta wire ran nationally under headlines such as 'Another Race War' and 'Negro Uprising,' stressing that Black residents outnumbered whites three to one.
The Watchman and Southron headlined the same telegram 'Negroes Hunted Like Beasts,' and the Worcester Spy 'No Negro Rising,' while the Wheeling Register blamed 'irresponsible negroes.'
The Richmond Planet ran the Atlanta wire in its 'General Southern News' column without headline or comment.

record_check.record: Bob Curtis, Carson Hardy, Colonel James Thomas, Small, Gordon
record_check.dossier: Charles Small (killed by a posse), an unnamed man reported taken from the guard, and unnamed whipped residents. Curtis was the white man whose killing set off the riot; Thomas was a posse member accidentally shot; Gordon was a white man burned by powder; Carson Hardy belongs to a separate Tennessee item.

record_check.record: Liberty City, Wayne County ... Negroes allegedly ambushed and killed Bob Curtis
record_check.dossier: Liberty City is in Liberty County; Wayne County was the home of Sheriff Lyons's posse and Col. Thomas. Curtis's first name is given as Robert, never 'Bob.'
One named (Small); reports range from one to five.
One named (Curtis); two in the Brunswick/Jesup dispatches.
At least three: Gill, Gordon, and Thomas (plus Bailiff Farmer).
Small and the whipped residents are described as Black.
Small was killed during an arrest attempt (in pursuit); 'taken from the guard' rests on one telegram and is unconfirmed.

record_check.record: accused of killing R. A. Curtis and wounding J. T. Gill
record_check.dossier: That accusation applied to Johnson and the men sought; Small, the one named Black man killed, was accused of breaking Tally's arm.
The fires were attributed by white papers to Black residents, not to the attackers; no one was burned by the mob. Whipping and shooting are supported.
